articles.title: A North Florida family permanently protected 816.46 acres with a $2.665 million easement; farming can continue while the land stays undeveloped inside a 1.6-million-acre wildlife corridor
articles.summary: US News: In the rolling pine forests and pasturelands of Putnam County, a North Florida family has made a decision that will change the landscape for generatio.
articles.body: In the rolling pine forests and pasturelands of Putnam County, a North Florida family has made a decision that will change the landscape for generations to come. They have placed a permanent conservation easement on 816.46 acres of their working farm, locking in protection for a sprawling tract of forests, wetlands and agricultural fields. Valued at $2.665 million, the easement ensures that the land will never be subdivided or developed, even as farming and ranching activities continue under sustainable management. The property lies within a much larger 1.6 million-acre wildlife corridor that links some of the most important natural areas in the Southeast. As reported by Action News Jax, the deal is a striking example of how private landowners can help safeguard habitat and rural character while keeping their land in production.A landscape of forests, fields and waterThe 816 acres sit in the heart of North Florida’s working lands country, a region where cattle graze beneath longleaf pines, cypress domes rise from flatwoods, and blackwater creeks wind toward the St. Johns River. The property includes a mix of habitats, from upland pine forests and hardwood hammocks to seasonal wetlands and open pastures. This variety supports a wide array of wildlife, including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, bobcats, black bears and numerous bird species that rely on large, unbroken tracts of forest and field. From a conservation perspective, the value of the land is not just in its size, but also in its location. It is part of a designated wildlife corridor that runs through much of North and Central Florida, connecting national forests, state parks, wildlife management areas, and other conserved lands. These corridors allow animals to travel safely across the landscape, find mates, reach seasonal resources, and respond to changing conditions such as climate change or habitat disturbance.The choice to protect while farmingFor the family that owns the land, the choice to put a conservation easement in place was not a choice to stop farming. It was a choice to ensure that farming could continue without the pressure of future development. Under the terms of the easement, the land remains in private ownership and can still be used for agriculture, timber production, and other rural pursuits. What changes is the right to subdivide the property into smaller lots or build residential or commercial structures beyond what is needed for normal farm operations. This approach recognises that working lands are themselves a form of conservation.Well-managed pastures and forests provide habitat, store carbon, filter water and maintain the open character that defines much of rural Florida. By protecting the land from development while allowing continued agricultural use, the easement supports both ecological and economic goals. The financial value of the easement was the difference between the value of the land as developable property and the value of the land as restricted, working land, and was appraised at $2.665 million. The landowner can receive financial benefits for donating or selling the easement (including possible tax benefits), while providing long-term conservation benefits.In a 1.6 million acre wildlife corridorThe bigger picture for this easement is a 1.6 million acre wildlife corridor that crosses several counties in North and Central Florida. This corridor is part of a larger network of protected and working lands that are meant to maintain connectivity for species that require large ranges, like black bears and Florida panthers. As development creeps in and fragments habitat, these corridors are more and more important to allow animals to safely travel through human-dominated landscapes. By adding their 816 acres to the permanent protection portfolio, the family has effectively strengthened an important link in this corridor.The property helps to fill gaps between other protected areas, reducing the chances that animals will become isolated in small parcels of habitat. For species that need to travel long distances to find food, mates or new territories, even a single large tract can make the difference between a functional landscape and a broken one. Conservation groups and state agencies have identified this corridor as a priority for protection because of its role in maintaining regional biodiversity and ecological resilience. Each new easement or protected area within the corridor adds to a growing mosaic of lands that collectively function as a much larger reserve.Benefits for water and wider ecosystemsBeyond its value for wildlife, the protected land plays an important role in the region’s water systems. North Florida’s flat terrain means that water moves slowly across the landscape, soaking into the ground, recharging aquifers and filtering through forests and wetlands before reaching rivers and springs. These forests and undisturbed soils on the easement property absorb rainfall, slow down runoff and trap sediments and nutrients that would otherwise wash into nearby water bodies. This natural filtration helps keep the health of the St. Johns River and its tributaries strong, which are vital for fisheries, recreation and drinking water supplies. They also provide a buffer from flooding by slowing the movement of water during heavy rains. As climate change increases the frequency of extreme weather events, these ecosystem services are even more important.The land also contributes to carbon storage, especially the mature forests and wetland soils. When they’re protected and managed properly, those places will continue to serve as carbon sinks, helping to counterbalance some of the greenhouse gasses behind climate change.A model for private land conservationThe Putnam County easement demonstrates how private landowners can take a leadership role in conservation without relinquishing ownership or traditional land uses. In a state where much of the land is privately held, the choices of individual families and ranchers have outsized importance for the fate of wildlife and natural resources. Conservation easements offer a flexible tool that can be tailored to the specific goals of the landowner while delivering public benefits.For other landowners in the wildlife corridor and beyond, the deal shows that protection and production are not mutually exclusive. It is possible to farm, ranch and manage timber while also committing to keep the land undeveloped in perpetuity.This dual focus can help sustain rural economies, preserve cultural traditions and maintain the open landscapes that many people value about Florida’s countryside. Conservation organisations and state agencies often work with landowners to identify properties that are especially important for connectivity, habitat quality or water resources. When a willing partner emerges, as in this case, the result can be a win-win for nature and for the people who live on and care for the land.Looking to the futureWith the easement recorded, the immediate work of protection is complete, but the long-term task of stewardship is just beginning. The land will require monitoring to make sure that the terms of the easement are being honored and that management practices continue to support agricultural productivity and ecological health. This may involve periodic inspections, coordination with conservation holders and adjustments to grazing, timber harvest or other activities as conditions change. For the family, the easement represents a legacy decision, a way of honouring their connection to the land while ensuring that it remains intact for future generations. For the wider region, it is a building block in a much larger effort to keep Florida’s wildlife corridors functional, and its working lands viable.In a time when development pressures are strong and natural habitats are increasingly fragmented, stories like this one offer a different path. They show that private landowners, with the right tools and support, can help shape a landscape where farming and nature coexist, and where the open spaces that define North Florida endure well beyond any single lifetime.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A critically endangered green sawfish swimming beside sea turtles wins Australia’s top nature-photo prize; photographer captured it with only 3% drone battery left
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In the sunlit shallows off northern Australia, a rare and ancient creature glided through the water, its long, toothed snout cutting a gentle path bes.
articles.body: In the sunlit shallows off northern Australia, a rare and ancient creature glided through the water, its long, toothed snout cutting a gentle path beside a pair of sea turtles. The moment lasted only seconds, but it was enough for a drone hovering above to capture an image that would soon captivate a nation. That photograph of a critically endangered green sawfish sharing the frame with sea turtles has just won the top prize in the 2026 Australian Geographic Nature Photographer of the Year competition. As reported by People, the shot was taken in the final moments of a tense field session, when the photographer’s drone battery had dropped to just 3 percent, turning an already difficult encounter into a race against time.A creature from another timeThe green sawfish is one of the most distinctive and threatened animals in Australia’s coastal waters. With a torpedo-shaped body and a rostrum, or snout, that can stretch more than a metre and is lined with sharp, tooth-like projections, it looks like a survivor from a much older ocean. These sawfish use their rostra to slash through schools of fish, stirring up prey from the seabed as they patrol shallow bays, estuaries and mangrove lined creeks.Once relatively common across northern Australia and parts of the Indo-Pacific, green sawfish populations have collapsed over the past century. They are caught accidentally in fishing nets, their fins are targeted for trade, and their coastal habitats have been degraded by development and pollution. The species is now critically endangered, meaning it is facing an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild. Sightings are rare and documented encounters in open, clear water are even rarer. The moment in the shallows The winning photograph was taken in the warm, turquoise waters of a remote coastal region where seagrass meadows meet sandy flats and mangrove channels. The photographer had been flying a drone along the shoreline, looking for signs of marine life that could be photographed from above without disturbing the animals. Sea turtles are relatively common in these waters and they often appear in aerial images as they surface to breathe or cruise between feeding areas. On this particular flight, the drone had already been in the air for some time, scanning the shallows as the afternoon light began to soften. The battery indicator had dropped into the red zone, a warning that there would be little time for anything beyond a quick return to the launch point. Then, in the live feed on the controller, an unusual shape appeared beside a pair of turtles. It was long and slender, with a distinctive snout that left no doubt about what it was, a green sawfish.Knowing the battery was nearly spent, the photographer made a quick decision to reframe the shot and capture the sawfish alongside the turtles before the drone was forced to land. The resulting image shows the three animals swimming in loose formation, the sawfish’s rostrum clearly visible beneath the surface, the turtles’ flippers tracing slow arcs in the water. The composition is simple but powerful, a snapshot of coexistence in a habitat few people ever see from this angle. A race against a dying battery The detail that adds an extra layer of drama to the story is the state of the drone at the time of the shot. With just 3 percent battery remaining, there was no room for error or multiple attempts. Had the photographer hesitated, or had the animals moved out of frame a few seconds later, the moment would have been lost. The drone might have been forced to land in the water, risking both the equipment and the chance to retrieve the images. This constraint shaped the way the photograph was taken. There was no time to chase the animals or adjust settings extensively. The photographer had to trust the existing framing, rely on the drone’s automatic exposure and focus, and press the capture button at the right instant. The fact that the image came out sharp, well exposed and compositionally balanced is a testament to both preparation and luck.When the drone finally touched down, the battery died almost immediately, underscoring how close the encounter came to ending without any usable image at all. In the world of wildlife photography, such near misses are common. The difference here is that the one frame that did work turned out to be award-winning.Why the image resonatesThe photograph speaks to several themes at once. Visually it is quite striking to see three iconic marine animals occupying the same frame. Sea turtles are loved by the general public already and bring the viewer into the frame. The sawfish is less well known but is clearly bizarre and beautiful bringing the element of wonder and rarity. On another level, the image is a reminder of what is at stake. The green sawfish is so threatened that many Australians will never see one, even while swimming in the very waters it inhabits. Capturing it alive, healthy and moving freely in its natural habitat is itself a kind of conservation statement. It says that these animals are still here, that their world has not yet disappeared, but also that their continued existence is fragile.The knowledge that the photo was taken with a nearly dead battery adds a human dimension. It points to how much wildlife documentation relies on being in the right place at the right time, and how easily such moments can be missed. That tension between preparation and chance is something many nature photographers know well, and it adds emotional weight to the image for those who understand the craft.Recognition in a national competitionThe Australian Geographic Nature Photographer of the Year competition is one of the country’s most prestigious platforms for nature imagery. It attracts thousands of entries from professionals and amateurs, covering landscapes, wildlife, underwater scenes and aerial perspectives. Winning the overall prize is a significant honour, placing the photographer among a small group of past recipients whose work has helped define how Australians see their natural world.Judges highlighted not only the technical quality of the sawfish and turtle image but also its storytelling power. The judges commented on the rarity of the subject, the clarity of the underwater view and the subtle story of three different species passing through the same patch of sea. The dying battery’s backstory added another element of interest, showing the unpredictable nature of fieldwork. For the photographer, the award is recognition of years of learning, traveling and pressing the shutter in difficult conditions. It also raises awareness of the green sawfish and the need to protect its habitat. Prizes like this can shift public focus, even if briefly, toward species that might otherwise remain invisible.A call to protect the unseenImages like this do more than win competitions. They become part of the visual record of a place and a time, influencing how people think about conservation. When a critically endangered animal appears in a calm, almost ordinary scene, swimming alongside familiar turtles, it becomes harder to imagine that it could vanish. Yet that is precisely the reality for the green sawfish.The photograph invites viewers to consider what else might be swimming just out of sight in Australia’s coastal waters, and how much of that world depends on healthy seagrass beds, clean estuaries and undisturbed shorelines. It also underscores the value of new tools, such as drones, for documenting wildlife in ways that minimise disturbance while revealing behaviours and associations that are hard to see from boats or shore. In the end, the image is both a celebration and a warning. It celebrates a rare encounter with a living relic of the ocean, captured in a fleeting moment when the battery, the light and the animals all aligned. It warns that such moments are becoming rarer, and that without continued protection of coastal habitats and strong measures against bycatch and illegal trade, future generations may know the green sawfish only through photographs like this one.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US strikes Iranian tankers near Kharg Island; Tehran threatens Gulf oil vessels
articles.summary: Middle East News: The US targeted multiple Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf on Tuesday, two US officials told CNN, in the latest escalation bet.
articles.body: The US targeted multiple Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf on Tuesday, two US officials told CNN, in the latest escalation between Washington and Tehran.One of the officials said the tankers were linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and were struck in response to attempted missile attacks on a US navy warship.The strikes come as the US intensifies its military and economic pressure on Iran, with Washington focusing its operations around the Strait of Hormuz. US forces have been escorting commercial vessels through the strategic waterway while maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports as part of a broader effort to increase pressure on Tehran’s leadership.Iran has vowed to retaliate by targeting oil tankers near ports in Bahrain and Kuwait.The IRGC, in a warning broadcast by Iranian state television, urged crews aboard tankers near the two countries to immediately abandon their vessels.“We warn all crews aboard oil tankers in the vicinity of ports in Kuwait and Bahrain ... to immediately leave their vessels, whether they are at anchor or docked at the ports, as the vessels will be targeted,” Iranian state broadcaster IRIB quoted the IRGC as saying.Iranian semi-official Tasnim news agency reported that one of the tankers struck on Tuesday was about four miles (6 km) from Kharg Island, a major hub for Iran’s oil exports. IRIB reported that a second tanker was hit off the coast of Jask and said crews from both vessels were being taken ashore in lifeboats.The latest strikes follow a US attack on an Iranian tanker about six miles from Kharg Island over the weekend.Separately, the Trump administration on Tuesday imposed sweeping sanctions on Iran’s aviation sector, targeting 27 Iranian airlines and nine service providers and sales agents accused of providing services to Mahan Air.The privately owned airline has been under US sanctions since 2011 and is accused by Washington of providing support to the IRGC.The latest escalation follows reports that Iran attempted to attack US navy ships on Monday. The US military has not publicly acknowledged the reported incident, according to the Wall Street Journal, which cited US officials.The reported attack came after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer over the weekend. No US navy ships were hit, according to US officials.The repeated attempts to target American warships have raised concerns in Washington that Iran may be using more advanced weapons, potentially with assistance from China or Russia.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Swansea cowboy builder tore my home apart and fled with £14k
articles.summary: Victims of cowboy builders describe how they were exploited with one couple left "scarred for life".
articles.body:
A rogue builder tore Sheri Ingram's home apart and "disappeared off the face of the earth" with £14,000.

In February, Lee Slocombe, from Swansea, was jailed for six years after defrauding nine victims of £400,000, with this his latest conviction in a decade of offending.

The UK government last month announced plans to give people greater protections against "cowboy builders" through a database of trusted traders.

Ingram, from Cardiff, welcomed it, but questioned where the incentive would be for tradespeople to sign up to the voluntary scheme.

Another couple who were "scarred for life" by a rogue trader who left them £30,000 out of pocket said it would give more confidence to homeowners.

"He (Slocombe) was recommended to us by a serving police officer who my ex knew," Ingram said.

"So why on earth would we have not trusted him?"

Slocombe's offending covered a period of 11 years, and he even targeted nine people to carry out work on their homes when on bail using a false name.

It began in 2015 after Ingram and her now ex-partner bought a house in Aberbeeg, Blaenau Gwent, which they planned to renovate and move into.

The then 21-year-old appointed Slocombe to build an extension and make the ground floor of the home open plan.

She admitted they were not experts in building work, and while it looked like lots was going on, Slocombe kept finding problems and asking for more cash to solve them.

While for the first six weeks, he was "very responsive", Ingram said he then "disappeared off the face of the earth" with £14,000.

Her ex-partner eventually managed to get hold of him, but he insinuated all the money was gone.

Slocombe suggested he was expecting a payout from an injury that he suffered on another building job, and would get the cash back and continue with the work.

The home was later restored by the the Channel 5 programme Cowboy Builders - aimed at helping families who have been exploited by them.

In February, Slocombe, then 33, of Delhi Street, Swansea, was jailed for six years after carrying out dangerous building work at properties in Cardiff, Bridgend and Swansea.

The £400,000 fraud cost his nine victims more than £547,000 in total when adding costs for rectifying his dangerous work, according to Cardiff council.

He had pleaded guilty to participating in a fraudulent business between March 2021 and May 2023, with one charge against him and one against his company, LSP Developments.

Slocombe was on Crown Court bail when these offences were committed.

It was the third time he had been given a prison sentence for offending that dated back to 2015.

That year, he was jailed for 43 months for three offences of fraud, and in 2023 he received a sentence of five years and five months after defrauding seven families of £150,000.

Cardiff Crown Court heard in February that Slocombe had called himself Lee Lewis to avoid his previous convictions being discovered, and on two occasions took a fake and unqualified gas engineer to properties, leaving them in a "potentially lethal state".

He was also made subject to a Criminal Behaviour Order, banning him from carrying out building, maintenance or gardening work in the UK for life, and disqualified from being a company director until 2031.

Ingram said the plans were a "good step in the right direction" as "the power imbalance is just so big" between people looking to renovate their homes and builders.

"There needs to be better protections in place, there has to be," she added.

"I would expect the government to take accountability if the project did go wrong if I used the database.

"I don't think traders would sign up and the reality is they don't need to."

What is the new 'cowboy builder' scheme?

The UK government plans to create greater protections for people renovating their homes against 'cowboy builders', through a new database of trusted traders and a payment system offering more safeguards.

Traders signing up to the scheme will need to demonstrate certain standards of customer service, transparency and dispute resolution.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unscrupulous tradespeople "leave families with months of stress" as well as unfinished work.

He added they gave their "decent, hardworking" counterparts a bad name and hoped to put "the cowboys out of business".

The UK government said more than a quarter of people who carried out home improvements in the past 18 months had experienced problems, such as builders disappearing after upfront payments were made.

It cited a survey carried out for the Competition and Markets Authority, suggesting customers lost more than £10bn in 2024 on home and garden maintenance services due to losses, overpriced costs or unfair practices by traders.

Barry and Shelley Sawkins, from Flintshire, lost more than £30,000 to rogue builder Christian Williams, who left their new extension unfinished, with water pouring into their home.

Williams, 54, is currently serving a two-year prison sentence after admitting theft and three counts of fraud by false representation involving four families.

In a Proceeds of Crime Act hearing in June, Mold Crown Court heard Williams, trading as Chris Williams Construction, benefitted to the tune of £163,051.70 from his offending, but his assets meant he could only pay back £1.

The extension remains unfinished three years after work began in 2023, and Shelley said this makes it hard for the couple to love their home.

"We're in a place now where we are stuck," she added.

They hope to eventually move to St Athan, Vale of Glamorgan, to be closer to their daughter once the work is complete.

"I really do respect him [Prime Minister Burnham]. I like his approach. He speaks from the ground up," Shelley said.

"I think the government plans would help give people more confidence."

The Federation of Master Builders also raised concerns over the voluntary nature of the scheme.

Chief executive Brian Berry said: "The prime minister's push to crack down on rogue builders is a great move for the industry.

"However, it is a real concern that this is just another voluntary programme without regulation behind it."

Minister for the future of work Kate Dearden was questioned on BBC Breakfast about the scheme and said: "We want to act quickly and get support to people as soon as possible.

"Of course if it was compulsory, that would take a little bit more time for us to develop and to work to.

"However, we are going to be watching this really closely in terms of the uptake and the impact that it has in the sector."

articles.title: South Park creators mock Trump's Lake Ontario rename and company compliance in mock statement
articles.summary: Trey Parker and Matt Stone announced "South Park" will be renamed "South America" Tuesday in a jab at Apple Maps and Google Maps over the Lake Ontario name change.
articles.body: "South Park" co-creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone mocked President Donald Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America, as well as Apple Maps and Google Maps acquiescing to the change, in a statement on Tuesday. "Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA. We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount -- a Skydance Capitulation," the statement on X read. The joke announcement followed the series winning an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program for its 27th season premiere in 2025, which featured Trump in bed with Satan while talking about his alleged Jeffrey Epstein cover-up. ‘SOUTH PARK’ CREATORS SAY THEY’RE ‘DOWN THE MIDDLE’ DESPITE TRUMP TAKEDOWNS The episode also mocked Trump's settlement with CBS and its parent company Paramount Global, which signed a $1.5 billion deal to stream the animated series on Paramount+ in 2025. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House, Apple, Google and Paramount for comment. Trump signed an executive order last month to rename the lake, which sits on the U.S.-Canada border, amid a breakdown in trade agreements between the U.S. and Canada. 'SOUTH PARK' CREATORS RIP SKYDANCE-PARAMOUNT MERGER AS A 'S---SHOW', BLAME DEAL FOR DELAYING NEW SEASON "The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes, including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario," the order stated. "Without the security and investment provided by the United States, this freshwater system would not be open for shipping, recreation, and responsible use to the same extent as it is today." FOX Business confirmed after the order that both Apple Maps and Google Maps updated their maps to display Lake Ontario as Lake America in response to the order. CHARLIE KIRK EMBRACES 'SOUTH PARK' PARODY OF HIM IN UPCOMING EPISODE AS A 'BADGE OF HONOR' Google previously said its Maps service would show "Lake America" to U.S. users after the update, while Canadian users would continue to see "Lake Ontario" and users in other countries would see both names. Apple users from these countries would see similar results. articles.title: NIA drops UAPA against American, 6 Ukrainians held in 'terror link' case
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The NIA has not invoked the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) in its chargesheet against six Ukrainian nationals and a US citizen.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The NIA has not invoked the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) in its chargesheet against six Ukrainian nationals and a US citizen in a case registered under the anti-terror law in April. The chargesheet instead invokes sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025.The chargesheet said the accused had valid travel documents but didn't obtain the mandatory Protected Area Permit (PAP) required to enter Mizoram. NIA said its probe into the UAPA aspect remains underway and a supplementary chargesheet may be filed if an offence is established. Special judge Prashant Sharma will consider the chargesheet on Oct 1.American citizen VanDyke and Ukrainian nationals Kaminskyi Viktor, Hurba Petro, Slyviak Taras, Ivan Sukmanovskyi, Stefankiv Marian, and Honcharuk Maksim were arrested in March at various airports for allegedly travelling to Mizoram without the required permits and crossing into Myanmar.An FIR was registered against them under UAPA over their suspected links to armed groups in Myanmar, where multiple militant organisations active in North-East India maintain bases. Earlier, NIA had told the court that the foreigners were being probed for a wider terror conspiracy, including allegedly assisting ethnic armed groups in India and Myanmar and imparting drone training to them.The chargesheet traced their movement from India to Myanmar from Dec 2025. They travelled from Mumbai to Guwahati and then to Mizoram without the requisite permit before crossing into Myanmar. Another group of Ukrainians arrived in New Delhi in Dec, travelled to Guwahati and then went to Mizoram to cross over to MyanmarVanDyke reached Delhi on Dec 12, 2025, travelled to Guwahati and stayed there till Dec 27 before visiting Mizoram without the requisite permit. articles.title: US accuses China AI developers DeepSeek and Alibaba of copying American AI
articles.summary: In its most detailed accusation yet, the U.S. government has named six Chinese AI companies that it says copied American companies for their AI secrets.
articles.body: In an alert published Tuesday, the FBI, the National Security Agency and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said top Chinese AI companies have systematically mined cutting-edge AI models from American companies since 2024, including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini and xAI’s Grok, to build their own. A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington did not immediately reply to a request for comment. The practice, known as distillation, is widespread in the AI industry, though it is often against AI companies’ terms of service. American companies and government officials have increasingly alleged in recent months that Chinese models are built by distilling American ones. The U.S. has accused China for years of stealing intellectual property from American companies. Tuesday’s report said the distillation campaign had come “likely with Chinese government awareness,” but it did not claim that China’s intelligence played a role. The White House frequently describes the U.S. as racing China to develop the most cutting-edge AI. President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept. 24. Officials from both governments have traded barbs in recent weeks over whether China has been inappropriately stealing AI trade secrets. The report accused six of the leading Chinese AI developers: DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI. It goes into significant detail, including a long list alleging that certain Chinese models distilled specific topics, like “legal specialization optimization,” “agentic functions” and “coach/assistant capabilities,” from particular American models. “The sheer scale of these campaigns and their sophistication indicate that distillation is not a supplement to these companies’ AI model development, but the critical core of it,” the report said. American companies have made scattered accusations of distillation since at least last year, when OpenAI said DeepSeek had “inappropriately” based its model on ChatGPT. In February, Google said it was inundated with attempts to clone Gemini but declined to name a suspect. The report also includes a list of recommendations for U.S. companies, including doing a better job of verifying users who pay for subscription services to American models and comparing notes with one another about suspicious behavior. It also recommended, in certain cases, downgrading or altering responses to queries believed to be malicious. In April, the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, Michael Kratsios, circulated a memorandum to the heads of federal agencies highlighting Chinese distillation of American AI systems as a critical issue. He wrote that distillation allowed Chinese companies to freeload off American innovation and circumvent safety guardrails built into American systems. In July, Kratsios declared on X that Moonshot had distilled Anthropic’s advanced Fable model to develop its Kimi K3 system. “Legitimate AI distillation used to create smaller, more efficient models plays a vital role in this open innovation ecosystem,” Kratsios wrote, echoing language in his April memorandum. “However, large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary U.S. technology and undermining American research is unacceptable.”

articles.title: Protesters, police clash in Albania over Trump-linked project
articles.summary: Albanians have protested for over 100 days against a planned luxury hotel linked to Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump.
articles.body:
Police in the Albanian capital, Tirana, clashed with protesters and blocked them from reaching parliament as the latest rally against a luxury development linked to US President Donald Trump’s family turned violent.

Tuesday’s march came as parliament resumed following summer recess and one day after the demonstrations marked their 100th day. Demonstrators challenged a police cordon in the centre of the capital, pelting officers in riot gear with eggs and tomatoes.

Since late May, angry Albanians have rallied against the planned construction of a vast luxury hotel in a coastal nature reserve, a project linked to Trump’s daughter, Ivanka, and her husband Jared Kushner.

Cars transporting lawmakers to the parliament building were confronted by the crowds and hit with plastic water bottles before police intervened to let them through.

Dubbed the “flamingo revolution” for protesters’ signs depicting the pink bird that could be harmed by the coastal development, the antigovernment protests have rocked Albania.

Preliminary work has already caused irreparable damage to a once-pristine stretch of Albania’s coast, destroying the nesting sites of both birds and loggerhead turtles, which are threatened with extinction, scientists and activists say.

Although Albanian officials have avoided giving details of Kushner’s role in the project, Ivanka Trump has spoken about her family’s involvement in the venture, describing it as an “incredible project”.

Critics say the project would also limit public access to the coast.

The nightly Tirana protests initially only focused on the development, but have since grown into a major challenge to the country’s long-governing Socialist Party.

Prime Minister Edi Rama, a target of the demonstrations, strongly supports the investment project, arguing that it would help modernise a country that spent decades in communist isolation.

Demonstrators chanted “Arrest Rama!” during the clashes, as police escorted lawmakers to and from the parliament building.

Several protesters were detained, but it was not immediately clear whether any arrests had been made.

articles.title: American Bishop Robert Barron calls out St. Paul's Cathedral in UK over nightclub partnership
articles.summary: Roman Catholic Bishop Robert Barron blasted St. Paul's Cathedral for its multi-year Fabric nightclub concert deal, calling it a surrender to secularism.
articles.body: Bishop Robert Barron criticized London’s historic St. Paul’s Cathedral on Monday over its new partnership with a nightclub company, arguing the venue's upcoming concert series undermines its status as a sacred space. The Christian Post reported that the Church of England is facing widespread backlash after St. Paul’s Cathedral in London signed a multiyear agreement to host concerts inside the building with Fabric, a nightclub company that lost its license approximately 10 years ago after two drug-related deaths. While the cathedral has worked with the nightclub company before, this latest agreement has sparked an international firestorm of controversy. Though St. Paul’s belongs to the Anglican Church rather than the Roman Catholic Church, Barron — a prominent American Catholic bishop — wrote a lengthy social media post arguing against misusing the cathedral. "Word has just come down that St. Paul’s Cathedral in London — the second most important church in the Anglican world — has imitated Canterbury Cathedral in permitting ‘raves,’ nightclub-like entertainments, to take place in its confines," he began. TOURIST'S CHURCH CLOTHING HACK LEAVES TRAVELERS SHARPLY DIVIDED OVER SACRED-SITE ETIQUETTE He blasted those who have already emerged to defend the move, saying "The usual reasons for acquiescing to this have been trotted out: reaching out to the young, trying to get with the times, etc. But this development simply shows that the leadership of the Church of England has lost any sense of the crucial distinction between the sacred and the secular." Barron argued that the whole point of a sacred space is that it is specifically set apart from the mundane, secular world and is meant to "reorient us toward the divine." "Accordingly, in the properly sacred space, one is lifted out of the conventional and introduced into the numinous. This is why Christian cathedrals are filled with images of the saints and angels and why their interiors are meant first to disorient us and then to reorient us toward the divine," he wrote. "The contemporary West is, quite literally, the first culture in human history that is in danger of collapsing the sacred into the secular, or better, losing any sense of the difference between the two," he added further. "This is doing enormous damage, especially to young people, whose lives have been flattened into a preoccupation with money, worldly success, and material things. The Church indeed should go out into the secular space to find those who have wandered away from God, but it should then lead those wanderers back to the holy." EXCLUSIVE VIDEO: BISHOP BARRON TO ADDRESS 'TRUE THREAT TO DEMOCRACY' AT TRUMP PRAYER EVENT He concluded, "Having ‘raves’ in the nave of one of the most sacred spaces in the Christian world is, I’m sad to say, another sign of our pitiful surrender to ideological secularism." According to the BBC, the events held at the event venue will be concerts rather than raves. "Under the partnership, Fabric will be the cathedral's exclusive partner for such events until 2030. The first concert is due to take place on 29 October, although the artist has not been announced," the BBC reported. "Fabric co-founder Cameron Leslie called the deal ‘an extraordinary and unexpected coming together of two very different parts of London.’" The BBC quoted Sandra Lynes Timbrell, the cathedral's director of visitor engagement, who expressed hope that a "carefully curated programme of exceptional concerts" would draw people who otherwise had not visited the cathedral. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The controversy mirrors a 2024 dispute at Canterbury Cathedral, which hosted sold-out 90s "silent discos" that critics mocked as a "rave in the nave." More recently, Canterbury cathedral featured the "Hear Us" art installation, using large stickers simulating graffiti, reportedly inspired by working with "marginalised communities and a team of skilled artists to create vibrant handwritten literature responding to the question: ‘What would you ask God?’" The project was conceived by poet Alex Vellis and curator Jacquiline Creswell. Fox News Digital reached out to Bishop Robert Barron and Saint Paul's Cathedral and did not receive an immediate reply. While cathedral leaders argue secular events help attract younger generations, some young believers say church leaders are misjudging what youth actually want. Catholic actor David Henrie recently told Fox News Digital that he sees young people turning away from secular trends and seeking out traditional faith. Henrie noted an uptick in youth attending traditional Latin Mass services in the United States specifically because they are searching for a clear contrast to modern culture. "I've seen it coming. I was one of those people who was not living a Christian life and then suddenly found the world was completely empty and was searching for something other worldly," Henrie said. "That's why I think you're seeing kids flock to the faith right now. It's because they're tired of the world." "[T]hey want 'Lord of the Rings Catholicism,'" Henrie said. "You know, they want bells, smells, ancient expressions of the liturgy. That's where the young people are flocking right now. That's why you're seeing the Latin Mass booming." Catholic leaders across the U.S. have reported sharp increases in the number of adult converts. A recent Gallup poll also found that 42% of young men now say religion is "very important" in their lives, a 14-percentage-point jump from the previous year. Fox News' Kristine Parks contributed to this report.

articles.title: TSA brings back gate access for some people without plane tickets 25 years after 9/11
articles.summary: The TSA is allowing eligible TSA PreCheck members without tickets to pass through security and enter gate areas, reviving a tradition that largely disappeared after the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago this week.
articles.body: LAS VEGAS — Airport security checkpoints have been the end of the line since soon after the 9/11 attacks for most friends and relatives who want to see off departing passengers. That is changing at some U.S. airports. The Transportation Security Administration is allowing eligible TSA PreCheck members without tickets to pass through security and enter gate areas, reviving a tradition that largely disappeared after the attacks 25 years ago this week. “As an exclusive benefit for our most trusted travelers, this new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way, bringing back the moments that once defined air travel,” TSA said on its website. The program, called “Gateside by TSA PreCheck” is free, but interested members must apply online one to three days before their planned visits and receive approval before going to the airport. If approved, they can enter security using a TSA PreCheck lane with an acceptable form of identification. The passes are valid for one calendar day, but reentries are allowed on that day. TSA says members of other trusted-traveler programs who have a Known Traveler Number also can apply for access to the gates. The program is initially available at 13 airports, including Los Angeles International Airport, Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas and Salt Lake City International Airport, according to TSA. The agency says it plans to expand the program to more airports in the coming months. Before the Sept. 11 attacks, individuals without tickets generally could accompany ticketed passengers to their gates. The attacks prompted sweeping changes to airport security, including restrictions on access to secure areas of airports.

articles.title: Ex-Colorado crime analyst who manipulated DNA data sentenced to 10 years in prison
articles.summary: A judge sentenced a former forensic analyst for the Colorado Bureau of Investigation to 10 years in prison on Tuesday after authorities said her manipulation of DNA data raised questions about the validity of hundreds of criminal cases.
articles.body: GOLDEN, Colo. — A judge sentenced a former forensic analyst for the Colorado Bureau of Investigation to 10 years in prison on Tuesday after authorities said her manipulation of DNA data raised questions about the validity of hundreds of criminal cases. Yvonne “Missy” Woods pleaded guilty in June to perjury, attempting to influence a public servant, forgery and committing a cybercrime. Dozens of other counts were dismissed as part of a plea agreement. Problems with the scientist’s work were found in cases involving homicide, sexual assault, robbery and other crimes, according to authorities. Prosecutors were forced to review hundreds of cases, and at least one murder conviction was vacated as a result of Woods’ misconduct. Woods had faced between 8 and 16 years in prison during Tuesday’s sentencing hearing before state District Judge Andrew Poland in Golden, Colorado. She resigned in 2023 after a decadeslong career. Authorities accused her of altering data to conceal tampering, deleting data that showed she failed to troubleshoot issues within the testing process and not thoroughly documenting tests performed in case records. Woods apologized during Tuesday’s hearing but said she knew saying sorry would not undo the harm she caused, the Denver Post reported. “For many years I was entrusted with evidence that could have profound consequences for defendants, victims, families and the courts. I failed that responsibility. I am deeply sorry for that failure,” she said. Following the sentencing, Colorado Bureau of Investigation officials said they have sought to reform their laboratories in response to the data scandal as they try to rebuild public trust. “The actions of one individual never define this organization, and they do not define the dedicated public servants who continued showing up every day with integrity,” bureau Director Armando Saldate said in a statement. The investigation into Woods’ misconduct began in September 2023 after an intern at the bureau discovered missing information in a case that Woods handled in 2018. According to an arrest affidavit, Woods allegedly told investigators at one point that she had changed data to complete cases more quickly. In the vacated murder case, Michael Clark was released from prison in 2025 after his lawyers argued that DNA evidence was mishandled by Woods. Prosecutors said they would seek to retry him. In two homicide cases, the defendants received lesser sentences under plea deals than they could have faced if they went to trial because prosecutors were afraid Woods’ involvement could lead to acquittals. Convictions in other cases also have been challenged in courts across Colorado. A Colorado Bureau of Investigation internal affairs report in 2024 revealed that concerns about Woods’ work first surfaced more than a decade ago. As early as 2014, a worker questioned her testing of evidence, and in 2018 she was temporarily removed from working on DNA cases after being accused of data manipulation, the report said. State officials have said that the response to Woods’ actions could end up costing more than $11 million.

articles.title: PSNI investigation of Creswell indecent exposure allegation 'failed victim'
articles.summary: The Police Ombudsman finds that "police failed the complainant, both as a woman and as a victim".
articles.body:
A Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) investigation into an allegation of indecent exposure made against Jonathan Creswell in 2016 was inadequate and failed the victim, the Police Ombudsman has found.

Creswell took his own life in 2024 while on trial for the murder of 21-year-old Katie Simpson in 2020, which he had denied.

The Police Ombudsman said it subsequently received a complaint from a woman raising concerns about how police dealt with a report she made that Creswell exposed himself to her.

In a statement, the PSNI said "the actions of the officers involved did not meet the expectations of the PSNI or the victim".

Creswell was a showjumping trainer and the partner of Katie's sister.

The indecent exposure complaint, made in January 2016, said the incident happened at a horse yard in October 2015.

Police Ombudsman director of investigations, Nikki Davis, said "police failed the complainant, both as a woman and as a victim".

"Indecent exposure is a serious crime and can indicate a potential for escalating sexual offending, so it is important that reports are robustly investigated," Davis said.

She said that "unless reports of sexual offences are properly investigated, victims will be less likely to come forward, offenders will remain free to reoffend, and efforts to combat violence and sexual offending against women and girls will be undermined".

The Police Ombudsman said shortcomings in the police investigation included that the officer initially assigned to the case recorded only one witness statement during the four months she was in charge.

No statements were obtained from three other witnesses, including a potential eyewitness.

A second officer subsequently allocated to the case did not get any further statements, and neither officer listened to a recording of an allegedly threatening voice message sent by Creswell, the Ombudsman said.

It added that the file submitted to the Public Prosecution Service for Northern Ireland (PPS) by the second investigating officer was also inaccurate.

The file stated Creswell was known to police only for motoring offences, whereas he had previously been jailed for violent offending against a woman.

It also incorrectly stated that there was no outstanding evidence and no other witnesses in the case.

The PPS then directed there was insufficient evidence to prosecute but advised if Creswell was interviewed about the allegation in future, the file could be resubmitted for further consideration, according to the Ombudsman.

The Police Ombudsman said when interviewed by its investigators, the police officer initially assigned to the case said she would have obtained the outstanding witness statements if she had kept ownership of the investigation.

The second officer, who was allocated the case five months after the initial allegation, said he had not been instructed to get any further evidence and believed his role to have been in a monitoring capacity, according to the Ombudsman.

The officer said he had not considered Creswell's previous violent offending to be relevant to the case.

"Indecent exposure is a non-contact sexual offence and a form of sexual violence, so the prior conviction was entirely relevant and should have been disclosed to the PPS," Davis said.

"It is widely acknowledged that police should be looking at behavioural patterns across incidents and seeking to identify where repeat offending might indicate escalating risk. That clearly did not happen in this case."

What else did the Police Ombudsman find?

The Police Ombudsman also found the officers had made inadequate enquiries to locate and interview Creswell.

It said although police had received information that he might be living in County Donegal and travelling regularly to Northern Ireland, the officers did not contact An Garda Síochána (Irish police) to check whether they might be able to assist in finding him.

They also failed to provide adequate updates to the complainant about progress on the case, the Ombudsman said.

The officers had, however, attempted to contact Creswell by phone, visited an address associated with him, made enquiries relating to his equestrian background and placed alerts on police systems about two vehicles linked to him, according to Davis.

What has the Police Ombudsman recommended?

The Police Ombudsman submitted a misconduct file to the PSNI, recommending the two officers should be disciplined for failing to properly investigate the case and not providing adequate updates to the complainant.

The Ombudsman said after considering the file, the PSNI determined the issues identified would be better addressed by taking measures intended to improve the officers' conduct.

Police Ombudsman investigators were unable to complete their enquiries into a separate allegation involving a different police officer who retired during the course of the investigation.

The complainant believed the officer was trying to stop her from talking to the media, the Ombudsman said.

Before retiring the officer provided a statement that he had called her to advise of the intended police response to a media query, and about how information about the case could be reported and used.

Although the complaint to the Ombudsman's Office was initially closed, a fresh investigation was started after further correspondence from the complainant.

The PSNI said it noted Wednesday's announcement from the Ombudsman.

"In this case, the actions of the officers involved, did not meet the expectations of the PSNI or the victim," a spokesperson said.

"We are committed to providing a victim-centred approach, and to learn from cases where our investigative processes have fallen short.

"We will continue to co-operate fully with PONI [the Police Ombudsman] in relation to any complaint."

Creswell was later charged with her murder. He took his own life one day after the trial began in April 2024.

A review, published in May 2026 , into how Katie's death was handled found "institutional misogyny" and "systemic failures" within the PSNI.

The Katie Simpson review, commissioned by the Department of Justice, found "not one officer thought seriously about abuse/control" in the initial police investigation.

The PSNI said it acknowledged the review and apologised to Katie's family.

articles.title: I'm 27 and I've already written my will - here's why
articles.summary: For many young people making a will may not seem necessary, but here's why you shouldn't put it off.
articles.body:
Writing a will is probably not on the to-do lists of most 27-year-olds.

But Erin Atkinson has already decided what should happen to her money and belongings when she dies.

"At first it felt quite surreal because you associate wills with older people," she says.

Erin works in psychological research at a London university and moved to the capital from Bristol four years ago.

She now rents and, although she did not want to share her exact salary, does not see herself as particularly wealthy. Even so, she has already decided where some of her things should go.

Her £7,000 car will go to her sister. A gold necklace given to her by her partner will go back to him. And she has asked for some of her money to go to a cause that matters deeply to her.

"One thing that's close to my heart is an endometriosis charity," she says.

"It felt really empowering that I could have that written down to say I want X amount donated."

For many young people, however, making a will may not seem necessary, particularly if they feel they have little to leave behind.

The 2025 National Wills Report found that just one in five 18 to 24-year-olds has a will in place. That rises to 33% of 22 to 34-year-olds, compared with 56% of people aged over 55.

Sophia Maslin, founder of Morby, an app that allows people to create wills online, says the idea that you need to own a lot before making a will is one of the biggest misconceptions she comes across.

"People believe they don't own enough. But actually, if you've got some sort of savings, investments, pensions, your social media accounts, if you've got pets, even funeral wishes, these are all things to think about," she says.

For Erin, the idea of making a will first came up when her friend bought a home.

Then she began seeing Maslin talking about wills on TikTok. Maslin had shared the story of her cousin, who died young without a will, and how complicated things became for her family.

Seeing her story made Erin think more seriously about making one for herself, while seeing the effect of her own grandmother's will on her family also influenced her.

"My grandma passed and she had a will and it was very complex because we have quite a large family. Seeing the will written in a way that was very directive showed me you can take a lot of pressure off the family," she says.

The process also made Erin see she had more financial assets than she realised, such as premium bonds.

Why a will can matter even when you're young

Eleanor Hodgson from Crombie Wilkinson Solicitors says there can be practical reasons for making a will even if you don't have that many assets.

"It's not just your assets that it helps because there's still someone that has to deal with your bank accounts and any debts you have, and it's [being] able to name a person that can legally deal with that without having to jump through hoops," she says.

The difficulties of not having a will can be hard to appreciate until the time comes, Hodgson adds.

Maslin says young people can be tempted to put off making a will, assuming it is something they will need later in life.

"The reality is that unexpected things happen at every stage of life," she says.

For Erin, some of the things in her will are worth more to her emotionally than financially.

Her will also sets out some of the smaller details she would like her family to know about, from a poem she wants read at her funeral, to the drink she would like served.

Thinking about those details did not feel morbid to her.

"For me, writing a will wasn't about expecting the worst. It was about taking responsibility and making life easier for the people I care about," she says.

Writing a will can seem daunting and expensive. But there are ways to get one written for free or at a lower cost.

For example, every November, Will Aid works with solicitors who volunteer their time and waive their fee for writing a basic will.

Once you have a solicitor, there are a few things to think about:

Choose your beneficiaries: Decide who you want to leave your money and possessions to, whether that's family, friends or a charity. If you have children under 18, you can also name guardians for them.

Choose an executor: This is the person who will make sure your wishes are carried out. It could be a trusted family member or a solicitor, but check whether they charge a fee.

Think about pets: You can say who you would like to look after them after you die.

Leave funeral wishes: You can include your preferences, such as whether you want to be buried or cremated, as well as music, readings or flowers.

Keep your will somewhere safe and make sure someone you trust knows where it is. If your will cannot be found, it can cause delays and may mean your wishes are not followed.

articles.title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony goes on for bereaved, 25 years on
articles.summary: As the 25th anniversary approaches, the wait for the alleged mastermind of the attack to be put on trial goes on.
articles.body:
The US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".

But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out.

Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back.

The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family.

On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center.

"After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind.

New Yorkers were 'lied' to about toxic air after 9/11 attacks, says Mamdani

New videos of man in 9/11 lawsuit reveal extremist links

Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious".

A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted.

Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants.

The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges.

Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028 .

But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial.

"My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said.

"Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added.

Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims.

Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about.

"I want to concentrate on the memories," he said. "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'."

Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died.

"They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones."

Mohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda.

He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z".

But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse".

He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial.

Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case.

"Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University.

She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions.

John Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case.

The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well."

During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office.

Relatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice.

"If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts."

Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial.

The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm.

Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing.

In court with the '9/11 mastermind', two decades after his arrest

The '9/11 mastermind' wants to plead guilty. Why is the US trying to stop him?

Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency.

Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions.

"My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are. I just want them convicted," he said.

Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal.

"It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said.

Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there.

"My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial."

With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event".

"I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended."

When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year.

Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in".

"If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained.

As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo.

"It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.
